Ticks, fleas and rodent-hosts analyzed for the presence of Borrelia miyamotoi
in Slovakia: the first record of Borrelia miyamotoi in a Haemaphysalis inermis
tick
Ivana Heglasováa,b, *, Natalie Rudenkoc , Maryna Golovchenkoc , Dana Zubrikováa ,
Dana Miklisováa , Michal Stankoa,d
a Institute of Parasitology, Slovak Academy of Sciences, Hlinkova 3, 040 01 Košice, Slovakia
b Department of Zoology, Faculty of Natural Sciences, Comenius University, Mlynská dolina B-1, 842 15 Bratislava, Slovakia
c Biology Centre, Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Parasitology, Branisovska 31, 37005 Ceske Budejovice, Czech Republic
d Institute of Zoology, Slovak Academy of Sciences, Dúbravská cesta 9, 845 06 Bratislava, Slovakia

A B S T R A C T
In Slovakia, little knowledge is available on the occurrence, hosts and vectors of Borrelia miyamotoi of the re-
lapsing fever group. In the current study, 2160 questing and rodent-attached ticks of six species (Ixodes ricinus,
Ixodes trianguliceps, Dermacentor marginatus, Dermacentor reticulatus, Haemaphysalis concinna and Haemaphysalis
inermis), 279 fleas belonging to 9 species (Ctenophthalmus agyrtes, Ctenophthalmus solutus, Ctenophthalmus as-
similis, Megabothris turbidus, Amalareus penicilliger, Hystrichopsylla orientalis, Ctenophthalmus uncinatus,
Doratopsylla dasycnema and Nosopsyllus fasciatus) and skin biopsies from 245 small mammals belonging to eight
species (Apodemus agrarius, Apodemus flavicollis, Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, Crocidura leucodon,
Micromys minutus, Microtus arvalis, Microtus subterraneus) were screened for the presence of B. miyamotoi DNA.
The overall prevalence of B. miyamotoi found in questing and rodent-attached ticks was
(23 positive/1260
examined) and
(31 positive/900 examined), respectively. Borrelia miyamotoi was detected in questing I.
ricinus, rodent-attached I. ricinus and H. inermis ticks, and in one male of the common vole (M. arvalis) in different
habitats (mainly rural) in eastern Slovakia. However, B. miyamotoi was not found in any of the tested fleas. Our
findings indicate that rural habitats with different species of tick vectors and hosts are appropriate for the
occurrence of B. miyamotoi.
1. Introduction
Borrelia miyamotoi, a member of the relapsing fever group in the
genus Borrelia, was first described in 1994 in Ixodes persulcatus ticks in
Japan (Fukunaga et al., 1995). The majority of relapsing fever (RF)
spirochete infections occur through soft ticks (e.g. Ornithodoros spp.).
However, a few RF spirochete species, such as Borrelia theileri, Borrelia
lonestari or B. miyamotoi, are transmitted by hard ticks (Rhipicephalus
spp., Amblyomma spp., Ixodes spp.) (Talagrand-Reboul et al., 2018).
Borrelia miyamotoi relies on transovarial and transstadial survival in
ticks and may coexist with Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato (s.l.) (Scoles
et al., 2001; Barbour et al., 2009). Small mammals have been indicated
as the reservoir hosts of B. miyamotoi in Europe (Burri et al., 2014;
Cosson et al., 2014; Szekeres et al., 2015; Hamšíková et al., 2017),
Japan (Taylor et al., 2013) and North America (Barbour et al., 2009).
Human cases of infection with B. miyamotoi have been reported from
Europe (Hovius et al., 2013; Boden et al., 2016), Russia (Platonov et al.,
2011), the USA (Krause et al., 2013) and Japan (Sato et al., 2014).
Borrelia miyamotoi has a global distribution and is represented by
three geographically separated clades/genotypes. The European geno-
type is associated with Ixodes ricinus ticks (Fraenkel et al., 2002; Richter
et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2012; Burri et al., 2014; Cochez et al.,
2015; Nunes et al., 2015; Szekeres et al., 2015; Kalmár et al., 2016;
Potkonjak et al., 2016; Venczel et al., 2016; Wagemakers et al., 2017;
Vaculová et al., 2019; and others). The American genotype is associated
with the ticks Ixodes scapularis, Ixodes pacificus and Ixodes dentatus
(Scoles et al., 2001; Mun et al., 2006; Hamer et al., 2012; Crowder
et al., 2014). And the Siberian (or Asian) genotype is associated with

The presence of B. miyamotoi in Slovakia was confirmed in questing
I. ricinus ticks in 2012 by Subramanian et al. (2012) and subsequently
by Venczel et al. (2016). Co-infections of B. miyamotoi and B. burgdorferi
s. l. found in questing ticks and rodents suggested that they share am-
plifying hosts (Hamšíková et al., 2017). In Slovakia, no clinical cases of
tick-borne relapsing fever have been reported (Public Health Authority
of the Slovak Republic, http://www.uvzsr.sk/en/). However, the
finding of B. miyamotoi in questing ticks and ticks collected from hu-
mans suggest a possible risk of this infection in Slovakia (Derdáková
et al., 2016). Of the 20 known tick species inhabiting Slovakia, six
belong to epidemiologically significant exophilic ticks (Ixodes ricinus,
Dermacentor marginatus, Dermacentor reticulatus, Haemaphysalis con-
cinna, Haemaphysalis punctata and Haemaphysalis inermis) (Černý, 1972;
Řeháček et al., 1991). The most common and epidemiologically the
most important tick species in Slovakia and Europe is I. ricinus.
In the present study, we aimed to determine the prevalence of B.
miyamotoi in several species of questing and rodent-attached ticks, fleas
and small mammals collected in urban, suburban and rural sites in
eastern Slovakia, as well as to provide a molecular and phylogenetic
characterization of the B. miyamotoi samples detected.
2. Material and methods

were collected at three sampling sites in eastern Slovakia during the
years 2014–2016. The first study site, a Botanical Garden with decid-
uous forest vegetation, is located in the center of the Košice, the second-
largest city in Slovakia

The live-trapping of small mammals was carried out twice each
year, in May/June and September/October, from 2014 to 2016, re-
spectively. Small mammals were trapped alive using Swedish bridge
metal traps following the protocol of Stanko (1995). Small mammals
trapping were carried out using 100 live-traps/per one night the same
for all studied localities. The captured rodents and insectivores were
euthanized in accordance with licenses from the Ministry of Environ-
ment of the Slovak Republic, No. 4874/2011–2.2 and 4559/2015–2.3.
The rodents and insectivores were identified to species according to
morphological features (size of body, tail, ears, legs, etc.), sex and age
classes (juvenile, subadult, adult) using the identification keys by
Pelikán et al. (1979); Sládek and Mošanský (1985); and Anděra and
Horáček (2005). An ear biopsy was obtained from each of 245 small
mammals and stored at

Each rodent individual was checked for the presence of ectopar-

were collected around mammal-trapping transects by dragging with a

2.2. DNA isolation and molecular analyses
Genomic DNA from rodent skin (ear tissue) and rodent-attached
ticks was extracted individually with the NucleoSpin Tissue kit
(Macherey-Nagel, Düren, Germany) and the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit
(Qiagen®, Germany), respectively, according to the manufacturers’ in-
structions. Genomic DNA from each questing Ixodes tick and flea was
extracted individually using the alkaline hydrolysis method (Rijpkema
et al., 1996). All DNA samples were stored at
{ \bf - 2 0 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
until further pro-
cessing.
DNA samples derived from individual ticks, fleas and rodent-tissues
( 5 \mu \mathrm { l }
each) were pooled. In total, 445 pooled samples from questing
ticks (198 pools), rodent-attached ticks (169), ear tissues of small
mammals (50) and fleas (28) (pool size 4–5 individuals for ticks; pool
size 10 individuals for fleas; pool size 4–5 individuals for small mam-
mals) were examined for B. miyamotoi by a real-time polymerase chain
reaction (qPCR) using B. miyamotoi–specific forward and reverse pri-
mers at 360 nmol/L, respectively, Brm1
-CGCTGTAAACGATGCACA
CTTGGTGTTAATC-
and Brm2 5′-CGGCAGTCTCGTCTGAGTCCCCA
TCT-3′. The corresponding dye-labeled probe (final concentration
100 nmol/L) was R6G−CCTGGGGAGTATGTTCGCAAGAATGAAACTC-
BQH1 according to a published protocol (Platonov et al., 2011). Sub-
sequently, all individual DNA lysates of all positive pools were in-
dividually examined using qPCR (Platonov et al., 2011).
All qPCR-positive samples were examined by conventional PCR and
sequencing. We targeted the 920-bp long fragment of the glyceropho-
sphodiester phosphodiesterase gene (glpQ) of B. miyamotoi with the
forward primer glpQ-BM-F2 (5' ATGGGTTCAAACAAAAAGTCACC 3′)
and the reverse primer glpQ-BM-R1 (5'CCAGGGTCCAATTCCATCAGA
ATATTGTG CAAC 3′) (Hovius et al., 2013).
PCR products were purified using Isolate II PCR and Gel Kit
(Bioline) and then sequenced. Nucleotide sequences were aligned,
compared and analyzed using the MEGA6 program
(www.
megasoftware.net). Nucleotide sequences were compared with
GenBank entries using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST)
(Altschul et al., 1990). Three newly obtained sequences from the pre-
sent study were submitted to the GenBank database.
2.3. Accession numbers of obtained nucleotide sequences
Nucleotide sequences of the fragments of the glpQ gene obtained in
this study from two I. ricinus and one H. inermis rodent-attached ticks
were submitted to the GenBank database and were assigned the fol-
lowing accession numbers: B. miyamotoi MN595157, MN595158 and
2.4. Phylogenetic analysis
Multiple sequence alignment was generated in MAFFT v. 7.222
(Katoh and Standley, 2013). Gaps were eliminated and the length of the
glpQ sequences was adjusted to 367 bp. The analysis consisted of 46
non-duplicating sequences in total: 3 were obtained in the present
study, 7 were obtained in 2019 in an independent study in the Czech
Republic, and 36 were downloaded from GenBank. A phylogenetic tree
was constructed using a maximum likelihood algorithm in RAxML with
100 bootstraps (Stamatakis, 2006).

host species (if relevant) and tick stadium, with consequent optimal
model selection in the Statistica software (StatSoft and Inc, 2013).

three habitats of eastern Slovakia. In the rural habitat Slovak Karst 8
species were identified: Ctenophthalmus agyrtes (49 ex.), Ctenophthalmus
assimilis (49), Ctenophthalmus solutus (35), Ctenophthalmus uncinatus (1),
Doratopsylla dasycnema (2), Hystrichopsylla orientalis (15), Megabothris
turbidus (17) and Nosopsyllus fasciatus (1); in suburban habitat Čermeľ 4
specimens: Amalareus penicilliger (15), C. agyrtes (54), C. solutus (17)
and C. uncinatus (11); and in the urban habitat Botanical Garden 2
specimens: C. agyrtes (2) and C. solutus (11). None of the 279 tested fleas
belonging to 9 species was qPCR-positive for B. miyamotoi.
3.3. Genotyping of B. Miyamotoi from ticks based on BLAST analysis of
partial nucleotide sequences of the glpQ gene
Analysis of the glpQ sequences confirmed the presence of B. miya-
motoi in ticks. In total, 24 out of 31 qPCR-positive samples were glpQ-
PCR-positive in rodent-attached ticks, and 21 DNA amplicons were
successfully sequenced from them. Twenty of these 21 sequences were
identical. The sequence (acc. no. MN595158) carried a single
nucleotide polymorphism, and the identity between this sequence and
the subset of the remaining 20 identical sequences was
The partial sequences of the glpQ gene of B. miyamotoi from 19 ro-
dent-attached I. ricinus larvae collected in eastern Slovakia were
identical with B. miyamotoi isolates (MF678600, MF678599,
MF576179, MF678597 and others). The partial sequence of the glpQ
gene of B. miyamotoi from one H. inermis nymph from this study (acc.
no. MN595157) was
identical with B. miyamotoi isolates
KY986528, MF678598 and others) identified in I. ricinus in Italy, Spain
and Hungary. The sequence of the B. miyamotoi glpQ gene from an I.
ricinus larva collected in Slovakia (acc. no. MN595158), which carried a
single nucleotide polymorphism, was
identical to B. miyamotoi
(MF678598) from I. ricinus from Hungary.
In total, 17 of 23 qPCR-positive samples were glpQ-PCR-positive in
questing ticks. The partial nucleotide sequences of the glpQ gene of B.
miyamotoi from I. ricinus (2 female, 3 male, 10 nymphs, 2 larvae) were
identical with each other and
identical with B. miyamotoi
(MG451835) from I. ricinus collected in Italy.
3.4. Phylogenetic analysis
Phylogenetic analysis of partial glpQ sequences of 46 representative
samples of B. miyamotoi with wide geographic distribution revealed the
clear clustering of them into 3 well-defined clades – European,
American and Asian – as described earlier (Fig. 1). While the well-
supported sub-clade consists mainly of B. miyamotoi sequences origi-
nating from China, Japan, the far eastern and eastern parts of Russia,
Estonia, Germany and Poland, the second sub-clade consists the se-
quences from the vast majority of states in Central Europe, Western
Europe and Southern Europe (Austria, Czech Republic, Germany,
Hungary, Romania, Slovakia, France, Sweden, Spain, Italy).
Borrelia miyamotoi sequences detected in the presented study cluster
together with the sequences from the second sub-clade. The separation
of sequences into two subclades is most likely linked to the distribution
of specific hosts or tick vectors.
4. Discussion
In this study, DNA of B. miyamotoi spirochetes was detected in
questing, rodent-attached ticks and one male M. arvalis captured in the
eastern part of Slovakia. The overall prevalence of B. miyamotoi found
in questing and rodent-attached ticks was
(23 positive/1260 ex-
amined) and
(31 positive/900 examined), respectively. The low
infection rates in questing I. ricinus ticks ranged from
to
which is typical in Europe, although a lot of studies have reported a
range between 1 and
(Geller et al., 2012; Crowder et al., 2014;
Hamšíková et al., 2017; Szekeres et al., 2017; Wagemakers et al., 2017;
Kubiak et al., 2019; Vaculová et al., 2019). The more frequent detection
of B. miyamotoi in host-attached ticks in comparison to questing ticks
could be caused by faster reproduction of spirochetes in blood-sucking
ticks, which increases the possibility of their molecular detection. It
might also be connected to the fact that the hosts were highly infected
with B. miyamotoi and blood-sucking ticks caught infection when blood-
feeding (Han et al., 2016).
In the current study, ticks infected with B. miyamotoi were found in
the urban habitat Botanical Garden, the suburban habitat Čermeľ and
the rural habitat Slovak Karst. In the rural habitat Slovak Karst the
sympatric occurrence of I. ricinus, I. trianguliceps, D. marginatus, D. re-
ticulatus, H. concinna and H. inermis was confirmed (e.g., Nosek, 1971,
1972; Hubálek, 1986; Heglasová et al., 2018). The absence of B.
miyamotoi-positive rodent-attached ticks in the urban habitat was
probably due to the low number of small mammals trapped and ticks
collected at this site. In the Slovak Karst, B. miyamotoi was found in all
developmental stages of I. ricinus collected from vegetation and small
mammals. The majority of the infected ticks were found on tested A.
agrarius and A. flavicollis (Table 3). Borrelia miyamotoi was also con-
firmed in one H. inermis nymph collected from a B. miyamotoi-negative
A. flavicollis. To our knowledge, this is the first report of the detection of
B. miyamotoi in the winter tick H. inermis.
Asian and American strains of B. miyamotoi detected in at least
seven species of ticks from the genus Ixodes (Hamer et al., 2012;
Mukhacheva et al., 2015; Cook et al., 2016; Siński et al., 2016), while
the European strains have been found only in I. ricinus (Geller et al.,
2012). On the other hand, Asian clade representatives of B. miyamotoi
were also confirmed in other species of ticks, such as H. concinna (Jiang
et al., 2018) and Haemaphysalis longicornis (Yang et al., 2018). Whether
these tick species play some role in B. miyamotoi survival or maintaining
in hosts still remains unclear (Cutler et al., 2019).
In total, only one of the 245 small mammals tested (ear tissue), a
common vole (M. arvalis) captured in the rural habitat Slovak Karst,
was B. miyamotoi-positive. This specimen did not carry any tick at the
time of capture. Due to the retrospective design of study, the skin
biopsy was used for the search of B. burgdorferi s.l. However, our results
demonstrated that this material is not suitable for the detection of B.
miyamotoi infection in mammals. Other authors recommended using
blood or blood-filled organs (spleen, lung, etc.) of rodents (Barbour

mammals (Apodemus spp., M. glareolus) were found to be positive for B.

(Burri et al., 2014;
Cosson et al., 2014; Cerar et al., 2015; Szekeres et al., 2015). On the
other hand, Hamšíková et al. (2017) detected a high prevalence of in-

) in the skin of A. flavicollis in Slovakia.
We analyzed 279 fleas belonging to 9 species for the presence of B.
miyamotoi, since fleas parasitize the same hosts as B. miyamotoi-positive
ticks. We did not detect any B. miyamotoi in fleas collected from small
mammals in the eastern part of Slovakia. To our knowledge, B. miya-
motoi has not yet been identified in fleas, which indicates that fleas are
not important for its survival or maintenance.
Phylogenetic analysis confirmed the already known pattern of se-
paration of existing genotypes of B. miyamotoi. All samples analyzed in
the present study formed well-supported clades, the clustering of Asian,
North American and European genotypes of B. miyamotoi. However, the
presence of two sub-clades among the European genotype was also
evident. While the sub-clade that included, along with others, the
samples from Slovakia formed the group connected to the main
European tick I. ricinus, the samples from the second sub-clade were
strictly connected to I. persulcatus, a tick distributed from the eastern
part of Europe to central and northern Asia, China and Japan. The
phylogenetic tree reveals a strong correlation between the genotype/
sub-type of B. miyamotoi and the species of ticks that transmit the pa-
thogen regardless of the geographic region: Asian genotype – I. ovatus;
North American – I. scapularis, West/Central European – I. ricinus,
Eurasian – I. persulcatus. As an example, the clustering of multiple
samples from Japan was defined by the species of their tick vector,
either I. ovatus or I. persulcatus (Fig. 1).
5. Conclusion
The presence of B. miyamotoi has been recorded in questing I. ri-
cinus, rodent-attached I. ricinus and H. inermis ticks, and in one common
vole male (M. arvalis) in different habitats in eastern Slovakia. To our
knowledge, this is the first report of evidence of B. miyamotoi in H.
inermis, and a tick species other than Ixodes from Europe, which may
indicate a wider spectrum of tick species for B. miyamotoi. The low
prevalence of B. miyamotoi in small mammals may be due to the type of
tested tissue. Borrelia miyamotoi was not identified in the tested fleas
belonging to 9 species collected from small mammals, which may
suggest that fleas are not important vectors for its survival and/or
maintenance in hosts. Our findings indicate that rural habitats with
different species of tick vectors and hosts are appropriate for the es-
tablishment of a local population of B. miyamotoi and its further spread.
We confirmed the strong association of tick vector species with the
genotype of B. miyamotoi that these species transmit.
